claims.text: Combining 70% cold rolling with rapid annealing at about 850°C for 30–50 seconds will induce a controlled dual-phase microstructure in Ti-doped Al0.7CoCrFeNi.
The proposed treatment will synergistically improve strength, ductility, Young's modulus, and fracture resistance relative to conventional processing.
The starting Ti-doped Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy has a primarily single-phase microstructure with minimal nanoscale precipitates.
A 70% cold-rolling reduction followed by rapid annealing for 30–50 seconds is a thermomechanical processing regime previously applied to medium-entropy alloys.
An annealing temperature of approximately 850°C is suitable for the proposed rapid-annealing treatment.
An inert atmosphere and strict control of annealing temperature and duration will prevent excessive grain growth or precipitate coarsening.
Maintaining Ti at minor weight-percent levels will ensure the desired phase formation.
The engineered microstructure will be effective at room and moderate service temperatures but may become unstable at higher temperatures.
The treatment will produce an FCC matrix containing a uniform dispersion of coherent nanoscale Ni3Ti precipitates.
The treated material will contain minor metastable BCC or beta-phase regions.
Severe cold deformation increases dislocation density and stored energy.
During rapid annealing, deformation-induced stored energy promotes heterogeneous nucleation of fine Ni3Ti precipitates.
Fine precipitates act as dislocation barriers and thereby produce precipitation hardening.
Ti addition induces local phase transformations that activate transformation-induced plasticity and enhance ductility.
In-situ XRD or TEM monitoring will keep precipitate size and distribution in an optimal range and prevent coarsening.
The treatment will increase yield strength by approximately 20% or more relative to cast or homogenized material.
The treatment will improve ductility by at least 15% relative to cast or homogenized material.
The treatment will produce a higher Young's modulus and better fracture resistance.
State-of-the-art cast or homogenized high-entropy alloys predominantly have single-phase microstructures lacking engineered nanoscale precipitate distributions.
Precipitate coarsening, inhomogeneous microstructural evolution, or service above the microstructure's thermal-stability range could negate the mechanical improvements.

contradictions.description: The product is called dual-phase, but the stated mediator contains an FCC matrix, a distinct Ni3Ti precipitate phase, and additional BCC or beta-phase regions, implying at least three phase constituents.

The prediction requires both at least 20% yield-strength improvement and at least 15% ductility improvement, whereas the mechanical falsification clause is worded to require both targets to fail simultaneously; failure of only one predicted target would not clearly falsify the hypothesis. No quantitative falsification thresholds are supplied for Young's modulus or fracture resistance.
